title: Moi aussi, je suis ta famille  (I'm Your Family Too)

segments.t: Mathias confronts Camille outside the agency about Hippolyte. He knows Camille is his daughter, but their colleagues still do not. Camille insists that she belongs to his family too. After the argument, Noémie declines her request for a light. Arlette then quietly offers comfort. Listen to the last scene of the episode in French first.
À quoi tu joues avec mon fils?
Je ne savais pas que c'était ton fils.
Il ne me l'a pas dit.
Tu es complètement irresponsable!
C'est toi qui mens à tout le monde!
Tu ne t'es jamais occupé de nous!
Tu ne t'approches pas de ma famille!
Moi aussi, je suis ta famille!
Tu as du feu, Noémie?
Merci.
Ne t'en fais pas.
Les chagrins, les hommes, tout finit par partir en fumée.
Let's take it slowly. Mathias walks straight up to Camille and attacks.
À quoi tu joues avec mon fils?

'What are you playing at with my son?' The opening is literally at what are you playing. Play can describe behaving in a way someone finds suspicious, as in English playing at. Mathias uses familiar you with Camille, whose family connection he is keeping secret.
Je ne savais pas que c'était ton fils.
'I didn't know he was your son.' Camille uses two past forms here for states that lasted: 'I knew' and 'it was'. With the 'not' around the first one.
Il ne me l'a pas dit.
'He didn't tell me.' Camille speaks a short sentence packed with small words: 'me' and 'it' both sit before the action word, inside the 'not'.
Tu es complètement irresponsable!
'You're completely irresponsible!' The long word in the middle means 'completely'. That ending often works like English 'ly'.
C'est toi qui mens à tout le monde!
'You're the one who lies to everybody!' Literally 'it's you who lies'. That's how French puts weight on one person. And 'everybody' is literally 'all the world'.
Tu ne t'es jamais occupé de nous!

'You never took care of us!' Never replaces the ordinary second negative word after the past helper. The action takes the helper be because it comes with the short self word. Of introduces the people Mathias failed to look after.
Tu ne t'approches pas de ma famille!

'Stay away from my family!' The French statement literally says you do not come near my family. Spoken forcefully, it acts as a warning without changing the ordinary order. My family excludes Camille, and her next line challenges that exclusion.
Moi aussi, je suis ta famille!

'I'm your family too!' Me too at the front insists on Camille's place among the people he has just claimed as his family. The ordinary I then starts the statement. The familiar your makes the reply personal.
Tu as du feu, Noémie?
'Have you got a light, Noémie?' Literally, do you have some fire? Fire here means a flame for the cigarette. Noémie says she does not smoke and leaves; Arlette then comes over with a lighter.
Merci.
'Thanks.' One short word acknowledges a small act of help. Camille does not need to name the lighter or explain the favour: Arlette has just seen what she needed.
Ne t'en fais pas.

'Don't worry.' The short it refers to whatever is troubling Camille. In this fixed expression, the action word do carries the meaning worry. Arlette offers reassurance without demanding an explanation of what happened.
Les chagrins, les hommes, tout finit par partir en fumée.

'Sorrows, men, everything eventually goes up in smoke.' Eventually comes from ends up followed by the next action. Everything gathers the two topics into one idea. Arlette links them to the cigarette smoke and suggests that the pain will pass. Let's hear the scene once more. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
À quoi tu joues avec mon fils?
Je ne savais pas que c'était ton fils.
Il ne me l'a pas dit.
Tu es complètement irresponsable!
C'est toi qui mens à tout le monde!
Tu ne t'es jamais occupé de nous!
Tu ne t'approches pas de ma famille!
Moi aussi, je suis ta famille!
Tu as du feu, Noémie?
Merci.
Ne t'en fais pas.
Les chagrins, les hommes, tout finit par partir en fumée.

The second episode ends with a painful family argument and a quiet gesture of comfort. Arlette's final image links the cigarette smoke with troubles that will eventually pass. Listen again to the shift from accusations to reassurance. See you next time!
À demain, Camille.
